sections.heading: EIP-8141 Spec Freeze and DevNet 0 Timeline
sections.summary: Spec is approaching freeze for DevNet 0; target spin-up is next week with Geth, Nethermind, and ethrex ready but Besu not yet.
sections.body:
- lightclient noted no major spec updates in the past week; conversations with Chris and others on L1/L2 interoperability improvements have not yet been upstreamed.
- The spec has been informally frozen multiple times but cross-client disagreements kept requiring clarifications; lightclient proposed formally treating the current spec as frozen for DevNet 0 with further changes targeting DevNet 1.
- Guru (Nethermind) confirmed the spec has been relatively stable and agreed this is a decent point to freeze.
- Client readiness for a DevNet 0 spin-up within ~1 week:
  - **Geth**: not quite ready today but can be ready next week.
  - **Nethermind**: ready now.
  - **ethrex**: ready now; passing all Hive tests.
  - **Besu**: not ready and no ETA; will not hold up other teams.
- lightclient committed to talking to the DevOps team to schedule DevNet 0 for Frames next week.
- No other client teams were represented on the call; follow-up to happen async.

sections.heading: Nethermind Spec PRs and Testing Progress
sections.summary: Nethermind merged shared opcode/mode lists across EIP-8141, EIP-8250, and EIP-8272, passed DevNet fixtures v01.0, and added an execution spec test for a gas accounting bug.
sections.body:
- Nethermind consolidated the opcode and mode definitions for EIP-8141, EIP-8250, and EIP-8272 into a single shared list to eliminate prior mismatches and speed up cross-client testing.
- Frozen DevNet fixtures version 01.0 now pass inside Nethermind's CI.
- A new execution spec test was added to cover a gas accounting bug on the "button roll reheal" path.
- Daniil asked other teams to review the open spec PRs linked in the [PM agenda issue](https://github.com/ethereum/pm/issues/2206).

sections.heading: EIP-8272 Recent Roots as Out-of-Protocol Canonical Frame
sections.summary: lightclient proposed moving EIP-8272 recent roots out of the transaction envelope into a canonical frame, keeping it as a mempool-only rule; no decision yet.
sections.body:
- lightclient argued that modifying the transaction envelope is high-risk and permanent, so if recent roots can be handled as an out-of-protocol assumption in the transaction pool (like the expiry frame), that is preferable.
  - Toni corrected the EIP number: 8272 is recent roots, 8250 is keyed nonces.
- Under this proposal, the recent root list would become call data to the recent roots contract inside a frame, rather than an outer list on the transaction object.
  - Nodes could statically reason about the contract's execution or simply execute the verify frame.
- Toni's concern: the root must remain statically available in the transaction so nodes can determine validity after reorgs. lightclient confirmed it would still be visible in the frame's call data.
- soispoke raised a gas concern: checking up to 16 roots via SLOAD costs ~40k gas, which would eat into the verify frame's gas budget.
  - Robert MacWha clarified the root should not be updated in the verify frame, only checked.
  - Toni suggested exempting recent-root gas from the verify frame limit since the limit is mempool-only and the behavior is deterministic.
- lightclient said an EIP would still make sense even if the feature moves out of the envelope, but it should clearly describe a transaction pool rule rather than a protocol change.
- No final decision; participants encouraged to think further offline.

sections.heading: ethrex Frames Testnet and Hegota DevNet
sections.summary: ethrex launched a permissioned Frames testnet open to other clients and a closed Hegota devnet with implementations of several additional EIPs.
sections.body:
- ethrex announced two networks:
  - **Frames Transactions Testnet** ([faucet](https://faucet.frames.ethrex.xyz)): permissioned, public for other clients to join (contact ethrex for deposit tokens). Implementation is up-to-date with the latest spec tests. Will be maintained until the official EthPandaOps DevNet launches.
  - **Hegota DevNet** ([faucet](https://faucet.hegota.ethrex.xyz)): closed, ethrex-only. Includes initial implementations of EIP-8250, EIP-8272, EIP-7805, EIP-7906, a Native UTXOs proof of concept, and EIP-8369.
- ethrex also noted the Hive test suite's frame-consuming tests have been stalled since August 26 and may need attention.
- Additional execution spec tests are being written and will be pushed over the next one to two weeks.

sections.heading: EIP-8130/EIP-8141 Authority Model Unification
sections.summary: Chris (Base) presented ideas for a unified transaction type supporting both EIP-8130's keystore authority and EIP-8141's code-as-authority, emphasizing no one-way doors and contract/precompile extensibility.
sections.body:
- Chris framed the core difference: EIP-8130 uses a keystore with defined interfaces to manage an external authority mapping, while EIP-8141 treats account code itself as the authority (via the APPROVE opcode).
  - L1 and L2 may differ in how much they absorb into the protocol vs. handle via contracts.
- Chris proposed generalizing the verify frame so wallets need not know which chain authority model they are on:
  - On an EIP-8130 chain, the verify frame routes to the keystore/authenticator with a known interface.
  - On an EIP-8141 chain, a selector tells the protocol which function on the account code to call for approval.
  - Derek asked why the selector can't just be the first 4 bytes of `frame.data`, ignored on EIP-8130 chains; Chris agreed that is likely a better approach.
- Chris outlined design principles: lean on contracts/precompiles over opcodes, use frame modes for generality, avoid new flags where possible.
  - An "AA precompile" concept was floated to handle 7702-like delegation, authority rotation ([EIP-8298](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-8298) mentioned by lightclient as a preferred alternative to EIP-7851), and other AA operations without envelope changes.
- lightclient pushed back on the strong contract preference, noting opcodes are easier to reason about and use from contracts; Chris acknowledged opcodes have their place.
- Chris confirmed 8130's authority model is not a one-way door and could work on L1; users could switch between keystore and code authority models.
- Chris and Derek committed to continuing collaboration and posting public updates; Chris shared an [Excalidraw diagram](https://excalidraw.com/#json=RFLiIvDMfjJBbWARoJB9I,TjZXEhjMq_TdX6h0tJ1d6A).

sections.heading: Signature List Placement and Aggregation
sections.summary: lightclient raised moving the signature list from the outer transaction object into a SIGNATURE frame mode, trading 1-byte scheme IDs for 20-byte addresses; no consensus reached.
sections.body:
- Currently, the signature list sits outside the transaction object, selected by a 1-byte ID (or an address for arbitrary schemes). This was motivated by:
  - Signatures being conceptually outside execution.
  - Reuse of the same signature across multiple frames.
  - Dano's push for easy stripping of signature data for future aggregation.
- lightclient proposed moving signatures inside the transaction as a new SIGNATURE frame mode, pointing to a precompile address. The main downside: every transaction would need 20 bytes to identify the signature scheme instead of 1.
  - Leading-zero precompile addresses would compress somewhat, but RLP/JSON overhead remains significant.
- Luca asked about similarity to [EIP-8288](https://github.com/ethereum/EIPs/pull/11772) (STARK frame for EVM execution compression); lightclient distinguished the two:
  - Signature aggregation is well-understood and likely to land sooner.
  - A full zkEVM inside the protocol is a much harder problem; not safe to depend on it for post-quantum signature aggregation.
- [leanVM](https://github.com/leanEthereum/leanVM) and [leanVM-b](https://github.com/leanEthereum/leanVM-b) (non-Poseidon version) were referenced as purpose-built zkVMs for signature aggregation, distinct from a full zkEVM.
  - Kevaundray clarified leanVM is a general-purpose zkVM, currently purpose-built for the XMSS scheme used on the CL and possibly inefficient for EL signature schemes; the team is looking at moving it to the RISC-V ISA. A zkEVM is a zkVM plus the EL state transition function, so "leanVM" as discussed so far is the VM plus the signature aggregation program.
- Taek Lee noted that SLOAD outside `tx.sender` is blocked in VERIFY for public mempools; Derek said this restriction would need relaxation to allow loading account keys from a keystore contract (associated storage).
- No decision made; lightclient asked participants to think about the data implications offline and continue discussion in the EIP-8141 channel on R&D Discord.

sections.heading: Max Verify Gas Limit for Privacy Use Cases
sections.summary: The 100k verify gas limit is too low for privacy pool withdrawals (~236k minimum); benchmarking is underway to determine a safe higher value, possibly adjustable without a new EIP.
sections.body:
- Mo Jahanara raised that 100k max verify gas is insufficient for privacy protocols; some teams are considering building alternative public infrastructure to avoid centralized private mempools capturing this flow.
- Nethermind measured a real privacy pool withdrawal requiring ~236k gas for proof checks alone (216k for proofs specifically). With up to 4 nullifiers, Mo estimated ~350k would be needed realistically.
  - kass noted that 250k+ would enable private transaction use cases.
- Toni and lightclient emphasized 100k is a deliberately conservative starting point:
  - The limit is mempool-only, not consensus-enforced, so it does not require a new EIP to adjust and can be raised stepwise.
  - ethrex made the limit configurable, defaulting to 100k.
- lightclient said experimentation with higher numbers will happen once DevNets are running; standard transaction pool optimizations should allow increases since the EVM is generally efficient.
- Nethermind is actively benchmarking to identify a safe upper bound; soispoke stressed the need for concrete benchmarks.
- Mo asked to share analysis and possibly present findings; the group agreed to continue async.
